h1: Becoming a beer tour guide or brewery host
title: Becoming a Beer Tour Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: What a brewery host or beer tour guide does, the brewing knowledge the job needs and how to get your first role in India.
teaser: A brewery tour is a ten minute brewing lesson with a beer at the end. The people who give it well are rarer than you think.
standfirst: Brewery hosts and tour guides turn a room full of steel into a story a guest remembers. The job asks for more brewing knowledge than most people expect. Here is what it involves and how to get into it.
sections: A tour guide is the brewery's first teacher

Most guests who walk into a brewpub have never seen a mash tun. A brewery host meets them, walks them past the brewhouse, explains what each vessel does and sets up the tasting that follows. In a taproom of 150 covers on a Saturday night, that might mean five or six short tours, each with a different crowd.

The title varies. Some places call it brewery host, some tour guide, some beer ambassador. In smaller Indian brewpubs the same person often runs tours, hosts tasting flights and helps behind the bar. In larger breweries with a visitor centre, it can be a full time role with a script, a schedule and a booking system.

What stays constant is the job itself: make brewing understandable in a few minutes without saying anything wrong.
The brewing knowledge you need is real, not decorative

Guests ask good questions. Why is the mash at 65 °C? Why does lager take longer than ale? What is that smell? A host who answers with confidence and accuracy earns trust for the whole brewery. One who guesses gets caught out by the homebrewer in the group. There is always one.

At minimum you should be able to explain:

  • The four core ingredients and what each one contributes.
  • Mashing, where enzymes turn malt starch into sugar, usually somewhere between 62 and 72 °C.
  • The boil, typically 60 to 90 minutes, where hops add bitterness and the wort is sterilised.
  • Fermentation, where yeast turns sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide, with ale yeast working warmer than lager yeast.
  • Why fresh beer matters and why heat and light damage it.

Our guide to beer styles is a good place to build the style vocabulary guests will expect you to have.
Telling the story without inventing it

The best tours have a shape. You start with the raw grain, walk through the hot side, stand in front of the fermenters and finish with the beer in the glass. Every stop has one fact and one thing to see, smell or touch. A handful of crushed malt passed around does more than three minutes of talk about enzymes.

The trap is embellishment. Tour guides are tempted to round numbers up, repeat brewing myths or invent history. If you are not sure the brewhouse was built in a certain year or that a recipe came from a certain monk, leave it out. Ask the head brewer for the real numbers: batch size, tank count, how long each beer spends in the fermenter. Real numbers are more interesting than legends anyway.

Timing matters as much as content. Most guests want 15 to 20 minutes on their feet before the tasting, not 45. Write your tour to fit that window, then leave room for questions at the fermenters, because that is where people get curious.
Safety is part of the tour

A working brewery is an industrial site. Floors are wet, hoses cross walkways, vessels hold hot liquid and fermenters produce carbon dioxide. A 1,000 litre fermentation releases a large volume of CO2 over several days. In a poorly ventilated cellar that gas pools at floor level. A good host knows where guests can stand, keeps them behind the line and never opens a valve or a manway to show off.

You also need to know the house rules on serving. Check the legal drinking age for your state, offer water with every tasting, keep pours small and make sure non-drinkers in the group have something to enjoy. Never encourage anyone who is driving to drink.

Hosting is a good entry point because you learn the brewery from the front. You see what guests like, what confuses them and which beers sell. Many hosts move into taproom management, beer training, sales or events. Some move into production after a few months of asking the brewers questions on their break.

If production is the goal, tell the head brewer early. Offer to help on a brew day or with cleaning. Hosts who show they understand the process often get the first call when a cellar role opens. Our guide to jobs in a brewery maps the other roles you will see from the tour route.
How to get your first hosting job

Few brewpubs advertise this role formally. It is usually filled by someone already on the floor, or by someone who walked in knowing more than the other applicants. Your edge is knowledge and presentation.

  • Visit two or three breweries as a guest and note what their tours do well and badly.
  • Write a five minute tour script for a generic brewpub, with real temperatures and times. Practise it out loud.
  • Learn to describe 10 common styles in two sentences each.
  • Bring that preparation to the interview. Offer to give a sample tour on the spot.

The gap most applicants show is in the brewing itself. They can be warm and confident, then stumble when a guest asks why the beer is cloudy or what a hop actually does. A structured grounding in the process closes that gap faster than reading forum threads.

Your first step: book a tour at the nearest brewpub this weekend, take notes on every question the guests ask, then check whether you could have answered each one correctly.
faqs: Do I need brewing experience to become a brewery tour guide?
Not usually. You need a solid understanding of how beer is made, good communication skills and a willingness to learn from the brewers. Many hosts start with no production experience.
What does a brewery host do apart from tours?
In many Indian brewpubs the host also runs tasting flights, helps behind the bar, handles group bookings and answers guest questions about the beers on tap.
Is a brewery host job a route into brewing?
It can be. Hosts who learn the process and show interest often move into cellar or brewing roles when they open, especially in smaller brewpubs.
